intro: Strauss sends Don Juan leaping up the violins in E major, then stops him cold in E minor. Albert Coates conducts this 1922 acoustic recording, originally spread across four sides of two records.

sections.label: A · The violins leap upwards
sections.mNote: A fast flourish launches the E-major theme

sections.label: B · The solo violin’s love scene
sections.mNote: A solo line opens into a broad orchestral melody

sections.label: C · The oboe’s long melody
sections.mNote: An oboe sings above muted strings

sections.label: Dev · Four horns and racing figures
sections.mNote: The horn call joins the opening’s restless theme

sections.label: Link · Harp tremolos and strings near the bridge
sections.mNote: Quiet recollections over a trembling accompaniment

sections.label: A′ · The E-major theme returns
sections.mNote: The violins climb again; the horn call follows

sections.label: Coda · A trumpet pierces the silence
sections.mNote: Trembling strings carry the music into E minor

cues.title: Up the violin strings
cues.text: A flourish launches Don Juan into E major. The violins’ theme keeps leaping higher, with quick notes rushing between its long, accented strides. Strauss gives his hero scarcely a moment to draw breath.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner describes the opening flourish and ascending E-major violin theme. Instrumental descriptions here follow Strauss’s orchestral score. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Lenau’s restless Don Juan
cues.text: Strauss prints three extracts from Nikolaus Lenau’s verse drama before the score. This Don Juan keeps pursuing a love that no single encounter can satisfy. The last extract finds the world empty and dark around him.
cues.evidence: Larner discusses and quotes the three Lenau extracts printed with the score. The Richard Strauss Edition introduction confirms Strauss’s explicit allegiance to Lenau. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20

cues.title: Themes in a Padua cloister
cues.text: Strauss later remembers that the first themes came to him in Padua, in the cloister of Sant’Antonio, on a holiday in May 1888. His sketches show he had begun months earlier. On his twenty-fourth birthday, 11 June, he tells his uncle he has “drafted a single-movement Don Juan”.
cues.evidence: Walter Werbeck’s introduction to the Richard Strauss Edition (p. XII) gives Strauss’s later recollection of Padua, the Italian holiday of 16 May to 10 June 1888, the sketches pointing to a start in about January 1888, and the letter to his uncle Carl Hörburger of 11 June 1888. https://schott-production.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/public_content/element/321495/dl/don_juan_einleitung_introduction.pdf

cues.title: One violin begins to plead
cues.text: The first love scene brings a solo violin forward. Its line pleads and lingers before the melody opens out through the orchestra. Don Juan’s upward-rushing theme will soon interrupt the singing.
cues.evidence: Larner’s score account traces the solo violin, the expansion of the first love theme and the main theme’s interruption. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Blue in the face
cues.text: At the Weimar rehearsals, the horn and trumpet players blow themselves “blue in the face”. Strauss tells his father so on 8 November 1889, delighted with the sound. Three days later he conducts the première.
cues.evidence: Strauss to his father, 8 November 1889, Briefe an die Eltern 1882–1906, edited by Willi Schuh (1954), pp. 119–120. English translation and première date in the Richard Strauss Edition introduction, pp. XIV–XV. https://schott-production.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/public_content/element/321495/dl/don_juan_einleitung_introduction.pdf

cues.title: Bülow’s verdict
cues.text: In 1888 Hans von Bülow, Strauss’s mentor, rejects Macbeth, and Strauss writes that Don Juan may soon join it in his desk. Bülow hears Don Juan with an orchestra at a Berlin rehearsal in January 1890 and sends Strauss a card praising the “magnificent” work.
cues.evidence: Richard Strauss Edition introduction, pp. XIII–XIV: Strauss’s letter of 24 August 1888 (“Don Juan will perhaps soon come to keep it company”), the Berlin rehearsal of 13 January 1890 and Bülow’s card, quoted in footnote 17. https://schott-production.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/public_content/element/321495/dl/don_juan_einleitung_introduction.pdf

cues.title: Four sides, two records
cues.text: Coates’s performance reaches its first owners on two twelve-inch Victor records, numbered 55176 and 55177. The music takes four sides. A listener at home has to lift the needle, turn a disc and eventually fetch the other record.
cues.evidence: The Animating Apothecary transfer identifies the two twelve-inch, 78 rpm Victor discs and joins their four sides. https://archive.org/details/1922-don-juan-richard-strauss-albert-coates-and-victor-symphony-vic-55176-77-4-sides

cues.title: Finished on 30 September 1888
cues.text: Strauss writes on the last page of his score: “begun in the middle of June, completed 30 September 1888”. It is his second tone poem, and he is twenty-four. Neither it nor Macbeth has been performed, and the first night is more than a year away.
cues.evidence: Richard Strauss Edition introduction, p. XIII: the inscription on the last page of the score copy, the completion on 30 September 1888 and the state of his unperformed tone poems. https://schott-production.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/public_content/element/321495/dl/don_juan_einleitung_introduction.pdf

cues.title: The oboe’s long confession
cues.text: A low-string serenade and flute replies lead towards the oboe’s long melody. Strauss surrounds it with muted strings. After the opening’s headlong rush, the score gives one wind player an extraordinary amount of room to sing.
cues.evidence: Larner describes the lower-string serenade, flute answers and oboe melody. Strauss’s letter of 8 November 1889 singles out the muted accompaniment in bars 232–307; Richard Strauss Edition introduction, p. XV.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A tone poem for Thuille
cues.text: Strauss dedicates Don Juan to Ludwig Thuille, who receives the score in July 1889. His first four tone poems go to the Munich circle around Alexander Ritter: Macbeth to Ritter, Don Juan to Thuille, Death and Transfiguration to Friedrich Rösch, Till Eulenspiegel to Arthur Seidl.
cues.evidence: Richard Strauss Edition introduction, pp. XI and XIV: the four dedications to members of Ritter’s circle and Thuille’s receipt of the score in July 1889. https://schott-production.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/public_content/element/321495/dl/don_juan_einleitung_introduction.pdf

cues.title: A storm of applause in Weimar
cues.text: On 11 November 1889, two months after taking up his post at Weimar, Strauss conducts the première. He tells his father it “sounded enchanting” and won a storm of applause almost unheard of in Weimar. The Musikalisches Wochenblatt counts three curtain calls.
cues.evidence: Richard Strauss Edition introduction, pp. XIV–XV: Strauss’s start at Weimar on 9 September 1889, the première on 11 November 1889, his report to his father and the Musikalisches Wochenblatt review. https://schott-production.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/public_content/element/321495/dl/don_juan_einleitung_introduction.pdf

cues.title: Four horns, one call
cues.text: Strauss gives four horns a broad call in unison. It joins the opening theme in the restless middle of the piece, where quick figures race around the larger melodies. The horn call will return at the last great crest.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner and Herbert Glass describe the unison horn call, its role in the development and its later return. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20; https://www.laphil.com/works/don-juan
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “Color is everything”
cues.text: In January 1892 Eduard Hanslick reviews the Vienna Philharmonic’s Don Juan in the Neue Freie Presse. “Colour is everything to them, musical thought nothing,” he writes of the younger composers. Young Wagnerians, he says, recall the piece with a “voluptuous shiver”, but to him it is “a tumult of dazzling blots of colour”.
cues.evidence: Eduard Hanslick, Neue Freie Presse, Vienna, 12 January 1892 (Nr. 9835), on the Philharmonic concert of the previous Sunday: “Die Farbe ist ihnen Alles, der musikalische Gedanke nichts”; “Wagner-Jünglinge … ein wollüstiger Schauer über den Rücken”; “ein Tumult von blendenden Farbenklecksen”. Our translations. Hanslick Online, Austrian Academy of Sciences: https://hanslick.acdh.oeaw.ac.at/c__1892.01.12.html

cues.title: A harp, a hangover
cues.text: Strauss calls this the “hangover passage” in his letter to his father on 8 November 1889. The score has trembling harp chords and strings played close to the bridge, giving the quiet recollection a thin, glassy edge.
cues.evidence: Strauss to his father, 8 November 1889, Briefe an die Eltern, pp. 119–120; Richard Strauss Edition introduction, p. XV, identifies harp bisbigliando and viola and second-violin sul ponticello at bars 447–457.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The violin climb returns
cues.text: The main theme returns in E major, with the violins climbing again. The horn call joins the final drive. Strauss keeps pressing beyond the point where this music might have made a triumphant ending.
cues.evidence: Larner identifies the E-major recapitulation, the horn call’s return and the continued drive towards the sudden break. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A London orchestra, an American label
cues.text: The orchestra is the Gramophone Company’s own Symphony Orchestra, not an American ensemble. Albert Coates conducts it in Room 1 of the company’s studio at Hayes, Middlesex, where the first part is made on 28 April 1922; take three is kept. Victor issues the set in America as 55176–77.
cues.evidence: DAHR matrix Cc1260 (Don Juan, Part 1): Symphony Orchestra [Gramophone Co.], Albert Coates, 28 April 1922, Hayes, Middlesex, Room 1, takes 1–3 with take 3 as master, issued on Gramophone D-670 and Victor 55176: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/2000007287/Cc1260-Don_Juan. The Victor 55176–77 set: https://archive.org/details/1922-don-juan-richard-strauss-albert-coates-and-victor-symphony-vic-55176-77-4-sides

cues.title: A trumpet and the dark
cues.text: A sudden silence stops the rush. A trumpet note cuts through the wind chord, and the violins tremble beneath it. E major turns to E minor. The last gestures have none of the opening’s appetite.
cues.evidence: Larner describes the silence, wind chords, dissonant trumpet, tremolando violins and E-minor close. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The solo violin opens a love scene
transitions.to: B · The solo violin’s love scene
transitions.how: An expressive melody first breaks into the rush at fortissimo. The orchestra then makes room for a solo violin, whose pleading phrases prepare the full statement of that melody. One player’s lingering line opens into the first broad love scene.
transitions.evidence: Gerald Larner’s score account gives the fortissimo announcement, solo-violin preparation and expansion of the first love theme. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20

transitions.title: Low strings make room for the oboe
transitions.from: B · The solo violin’s love scene
transitions.how: The upward-rushing theme interrupts the first love scene. In the next, violas and cellos begin a serenade, answered by the flute. The oboe then takes the long melody above muted strings, stretching its phrases across the quiet accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Larner traces the intervening main theme, low-string serenade, flute and oboe. The Richard Strauss Edition introduction, p. XV, identifies the muted oboe passage as bars 232–307.

transitions.title: The horn call takes command
transitions.to: Dev · Four horns and racing figures
transitions.how: A broad unison call for four horns carries Don Juan away from the oboe’s love scene. Marked sehr energisch, it becomes a partner to the opening theme in the development. Quick orchestral figures gather around these two large ideas.
transitions.evidence: Larner describes the horn call’s emergence and role in the development; Herbert Glass gives sehr energisch and the four horns in unison. https://www.laphil.com/works/don-juan

transitions.title: The harp trembles under a recollection
transitions.from: Dev · Four horns and racing figures
transitions.to: Link · Harp tremolos and strings near the bridge
transitions.how: The driven middle gives way to quiet recollections of the love music. Strauss writes trembling chords for the harp and asks the violas and second violins to bow close to the bridge. Their thin sound leaves the remembered melodies exposed.
transitions.evidence: Larner identifies the quiet recollections near the end of the development. Richard Strauss Edition introduction, p. XV, specifies harp bisbigliando and strings sul ponticello in bars 447–457.

transitions.title: The violins recover E major
transitions.from: Link · Harp tremolos and strings near the bridge
transitions.how: The quiet recollections release the main theme in E major. The violins restore their upward leaps and the orchestra gathers behind them. The horn call returns later in the drive, bringing the work’s two most forceful themes into its closing stretch.
transitions.evidence: Gerald Larner’s account identifies the E-major recapitulation and the horn call in the closing climax.

transitions.title: Silence, then a dissonant trumpet
transitions.to: Coda · A trumpet pierces the silence
transitions.how: The rushing music breaks off. Wind chords enter the silence, pierced by a dissonant trumpet note, and the violins continue in tremolo. E remains the home note, but the chord turns minor. The orchestra spends its remaining phrases quietly.
transitions.evidence: Gerald Larner describes the final silence, wind chord, trumpet dissonance, string tremolo and E-minor close. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20

composer.epithet: The son of a horn player, he gave the orchestra a taste for scandal and the soprano some of her longest, loveliest farewells.
facts: Munich, with Friedrich Wilhelm Meyer; conducting with Hans von Bülow at Meiningen
Munich · Weimar · Berlin Court Opera, 1898–1918 · Vienna State Opera, 1919–24
Tone poems, fifteen operas, two horn concertos and more than two hundred songs
composer.background:
Richard Strauss grew up with the horn in his ears. His father Franz played in the Munich Court Orchestra, including the first performances of Wagner’s Tristan and Die Meistersinger, and detested the music. At home, Mozart stood above everybody; Haydn and Beethoven were safe too. Richard, born in 1864, had piano lessons from the age of four and was composing at six. His mother Josepha came from the Pschorr brewing family. He studied privately with Friedrich Wilhelm Meyer and learnt the sound of an orchestra from the men his father worked beside.

Hans von Bülow took him to Meiningen in 1885. At twenty-one he had an orchestra of his own to rehearse, as well as a choir and a princess to teach. The violinist Alexander Ritter, married to Wagner’s niece, completed his conversion to the music his father disliked. Ritter also urged Liszt’s symphonic poems upon him. Strauss would spend the next decade finding out how much a concert orchestra could tell us about a man without letting the man sing.
